title: Transformer Attention Lab
description: Work through a complete attention head: tensor shapes, scaled logits, stable softmax, causal masking and the cost of a longer context. Original examples for readers comfortable with vectors.

sections.title: Queries, keys and values
sections.body:
Start with a sequence represented by X, a T × d_model matrix. One attention head learns three projections: Q = X W_Q, K = X W_K and V = X W_V. For this head, Q and K have width d_k; V has width d_v. Multiplying Q Kᵀ produces one score for every query/key pair, so its shape is T × T. The output of softmax(Q Kᵀ / √d_k) V has shape T × d_v.

A query asks which positions matter for its current representation. A key participates in the matching score. A value supplies the vector that is mixed into the output. These roles describe the computation; they are not three separate copies of a sentence stored in a database.

For the following example, use one query and three keys. Choose d_k = 2 and d_v = 2. The query is q = [√2, 0]. The keys are k₁ = [1, 0], k₂ = [0, 1] and k₃ = [1, 1]. The values are v₁ = [1, 0], v₂ = [0, 2] and v₃ = [3, 1]. These independently chosen vectors are an arithmetic example, not activations recorded from a trained language model.

sections.title: Compute one attention output
sections.body:
The raw dot products for our query are [√2, 0, √2]. Divide by √d_k = √2 to obtain the logits s = [1, 0, 1].

Stable softmax subtracts the largest logit before exponentiation. Here the exponentials become [1, exp(−1), 1]. Their sum is approximately 2.367879441. The resulting attention weights are approximately [0.4223187983, 0.1553624035, 0.4223187983]. Subtracting the maximum changes neither the mathematical probabilities nor their sum; it prevents avoidable overflow in a numerical implementation.

Now mix the values coordinate by coordinate:
o₁ = 0.4223187983 × 1 + 0.1553624035 × 0 + 0.4223187983 × 3
   ≈ 1.6892751930
o₂ = 0.4223187983 × 0 + 0.1553624035 × 2 + 0.4223187983 × 1
   ≈ 0.7330436052

The result is the vector [1.6892751930, 0.7330436052], not the most-attended token's ID. Attention creates a weighted representation. Later projections and network layers still have work to do.

The √d_k factor controls dot-product scale under common initialization assumptions. It is not a guarantee about all trained score distributions.

sections.title: Apply a causal mask
sections.body:
Suppose this query is at the second position of a three-token sequence during autoregressive training. It may attend to positions one and two, but position three is in its future. Apply the mask to the logits before softmax: [1, 0, −∞]. The masked exponential is zero, so the weights become approximately [0.7310585786, 0.2689414214, 0].

With the same values, the new output is approximately [0.7310585786, 0.5378828427]. Masking after softmax without renormalizing would leave weights that do not sum to one and produce a different computation.

The mask is about information access. Multiplying a future value by a small nonzero probability still leaks future information. Padding positions need suitable masking too. A row with every key masked has no valid probability distribution; a production implementation needs an explicit policy for that case.

In the interactive lab, enabling the causal mask hides the third key for this one query. A complete decoder constructs a corresponding mask for every query row.

sections.title: Context cost and what attention does not prove
sections.body:
An explicitly materialized dense score matrix has T² entries per head. At T = 4096, that is 16,777,216 entries. At two bytes per entry, one head's score matrix alone occupies 33,554,432 bytes, or 32 MiB. Doubling T to 8192 gives 67,108,864 entries and 128 MiB per head: four times the score storage.

This is a count of one explicit matrix. It excludes Q/K/V, other heads, layers, gradients, optimizer state and temporary buffers. Kernels can avoid storing the entire score matrix, so do not treat this worksheet as a prediction of a particular model's GPU usage.

The computation above does not establish that a token caused a prediction, that the network understood the sentence, or that an attention weight is a complete feature attribution. It isolates one operation so its mechanics can be checked.

Primary reference: Vaswani and colleagues, Attention Is All You Need (2017), arXiv:1706.03762. This original study guide and its chosen numerical examples are CC0; the cited paper retains its own license.
